title: Working Capital in Private Equity
summary: Working Capital in Private Equity explains why receivables, inventory, and payables become board-level levers for cash, debt paydown, and valuation.
definition: Working capital is the cash tied up in day-to-day operations, primarily accounts receivable, inventory, and accounts payable.
whyItMatters: PE operators treat working capital as trapped cash that can fund debt paydown, add-ons, transformation, or liquidity protection.
example: A distributor that reduces inventory days and accelerates collections can release cash without growing revenue or raising new capital.

articleSections.title: Translate the Cash Conversion Cycle into Sponsor Economics
body: Working capital converts operating activity into either available cash or a financing requirement. For most industrial, distribution, and service businesses, the core operating components are accounts receivable plus inventory minus accounts payable, with other current accounts included only when their economics belong to normal operations. Days sales outstanding measures the time to collect revenue, days inventory outstanding measures how long cost sits in stock, and days payable outstanding measures supplier financing. The cash conversion cycle equals DSO plus DIO minus DPO. A shorter cycle generally releases cash, but the improvement is valuable only when collections, service, supply continuity, and margins remain healthy.

Cash conversion is especially important in a leveraged company because EBITDA does not repay debt. Growth can consume cash when receivables and inventory expand faster than payables, even while reported profit rises. A seasonal business can be covenant-compliant at year-end and still breach its revolver capacity during the peak build. The underwriting model should therefore link revenue and cost growth to working-capital days by month, not apply a flat annual percentage. The thirteen-week cash forecast then connects collections, purchasing, payroll, taxes, interest, and capex to actual liquidity and identifies the earliest point at which management must intervene.

Ownership must be operational as well as financial. The CFO owns cash forecasting and the balance-sheet truth; the controller owns reconciliations and aging; sales leaders own customer terms and dispute escalation; operations and supply chain own inventory; procurement owns supplier terms; and business-unit leaders own exceptions. Treasury may coordinate daily cash, but it cannot fix late billing or excess safety stock alone. Weekly cash and aging reviews, monthly operating reviews, and quarterly board oversight create a cadence. Gates should protect minimum liquidity, covenant headroom, service levels, supplier continuity, and control quality before a cash-release target is counted.
articleSections.callout: Working-capital value is the durable cash released after protecting customers, suppliers, service levels, and the next operating cycle.

articleSections.title: Normalize Transaction Net Working Capital
body: At acquisition and exit, the normalized net working capital peg separates the enterprise-value bargain from the capital delivered with the business. The agreement defines included accounts and compares closing working capital with a negotiated normal level. If closing working capital is below the peg, equity value generally falls dollar for dollar; if above, it generally rises. The peg should reflect ordinary seasonality, growth, accounting policies, aging quality, and business mix. A trailing average is useful evidence but not an answer when acquisitions, price inflation, unusual customer timing, or a seasonal close distort historical balances.

The schedule must avoid double counting with cash, debt, debt-like items, and QoE adjustments. Overdue payables classified as debt-like cannot also reduce closing net working capital. Restricted cash is not an operating receivable. Deferred revenue requires consistent treatment based on the future performance obligation and historical peg methodology. Reserves for doubtful accounts, returns, obsolescence, rebates, and warranties should follow the purchase agreement's accounting hierarchy rather than changing opportunistically at close. Finance should map every relevant general-ledger account to one category and reconcile monthly source data to the financial statements before negotiations harden.

A cross-functional peg review should begin during diligence. Finance produces monthly balances and policies; commercial leaders explain customer and billing patterns; supply chain explains inventory builds; procurement validates payment cycles; and the deal team owns the negotiated outcome. Review gates include aging and reserve quality, seasonal peak funding, consistency with the QoE, and a Day One liquidity forecast. Failure modes include selecting only low working-capital months, comparing gross historical balances with net closing balances, treating a temporary collections push as normal, or embedding an unproven future improvement in the peg. The buyer should pay for delivered capital, not for a plan it must execute after close.

articleSections.title: Improve Receivables, Inventory, and Payables by Segment
body: Receivables performance should be segmented by customer, business unit, invoice type, aging bucket, dispute code, and collector. The levers are upstream as often as they are downstream: credit approval, contract terms, proof of delivery, billing speed, invoice accuracy, electronic submission, collections cadence, and executive escalation. A collector cannot recover days lost because a project manager failed to approve a milestone. Dashboards should show current, past due, disputed, promised, and unapplied cash separately. Gates include credit limits for new orders, same-day escalation of material disputes, and a defined approval authority for term exceptions and write-offs.

Inventory requires segmentation because aggregate turns conceal very different economics. ABC classification identifies value concentration; XYZ or demand-variability analysis identifies forecastability; lifecycle flags separate launch, active, slow-moving, excess, and obsolete stock; and location views expose duplicate buffers. Operations should set service-level targets and replenishment policies by segment, then address supplier lead time, minimum order quantities, batch size, forecast bias, yield, and SKU complexity. A blanket inventory cut can create stockouts while leaving obsolete items untouched. Cash is counted only when purchasing is reduced or inventory is sold, consumed, returned, or disposed of—not when a spreadsheet target changes.

Payables improvement begins with accurate supplier masters, contracted terms, invoice receipt, three-way matching, approval workflow, and payment-date discipline. Paying on the due date is different from indiscriminately paying late. Procurement can negotiate terms using spend concentration and supplier economics, while accounts payable eliminates early payment caused by poor controls. Supplier segmentation protects sole-source, capacity-constrained, and financially fragile vendors from a uniform extension mandate. Metrics should pair DPO with on-time payment, blocked invoices, early-payment discounts, supplier complaints, and price changes. A ten-day DPO gain that triggers supply interruption or a two-percent price increase destroys value rather than creating it.

articleSections.title: Operate a Controlled Cash Cadence with Named Owners
body: A practical cadence starts with a daily cash position and critical exceptions, a weekly thirteen-week forecast and working-capital war room, a monthly close and driver review, and a quarterly board assessment of conversion and liquidity. The weekly meeting should review promised collections, top disputes, inventory exceptions, purchase commitments, overdue approvals, supplier risks, and forecast variance. Each action needs an owner, amount, due date, dependency, and confidence level. The CFO chairs the cash process, but functional leaders commit actions. The operating partner challenges the trajectory and removes cross-functional blockers rather than becoming a substitute collections manager.

Controls prevent a cash initiative from creating accounting or commercial damage. Bank and subledger reconciliations establish the baseline; segregation of duties protects customer credits, supplier-master changes, and payments; approval matrices govern terms, purchases, write-offs, and inventory dispositions; and data definitions keep KPIs comparable. Incentives should balance cash with revenue quality, gross margin, fill rate, retention, and supplier service. Sales compensation based only on bookings invites weak credit and long terms. Procurement savings based only on DPO invites late payments. Inventory bonuses based only on days invite stockouts and deferred purchasing around measurement dates.

Management should establish escalation gates before a crisis. Examples include a minimum cash floor, revolver availability threshold, covenant cushion, receivable aging limit, inventory service floor, and critical-supplier risk flag. Breaching a gate triggers a predefined action set and decision authority: freeze discretionary spend, intensify collections, revise purchasing, draw liquidity, or involve lenders. Common failures include treating a one-time cleanup as a permanent process, using average days that hide tail risk, rewarding gross cash without offsets, and confusing forecast timing with structural improvement. Sustainability requires repeated performance through a full seasonal cycle.

articleSections.title: Reconcile Cash Release to Covenants and Exit Sustainability
body: A numeric bridge converts days into dollars. Assume annual revenue of $120 million and cost of goods sold of $72 million. Reducing DSO from 60 to 48 days releases about $3.95 million: twelve days multiplied by $120 million divided by 365. Reducing DIO from 90 to 75 days releases about $2.96 million: fifteen days multiplied by $72 million divided by 365. Increasing DPO from 35 to 45 days releases about $1.97 million: ten days multiplied by $72 million divided by 365. The cash conversion cycle falls from 115 to 78 days, and total gross cash release is approximately $8.88 million.

The $8.88 million is not EBITDA and should not be multiplied in valuation. It is a balance-sheet release that may repay debt, fund an acquisition, or protect liquidity. If all proceeds reduce debt, equity value at a constant enterprise value rises by the amount of lower net debt, subject to taxes, fees, leakage, and any minimum cash requirement. Lower debt can also improve fixed-charge coverage and covenant headroom, but definitions in the credit agreement control. The base case should phase benefits by driver, include implementation costs and growth requirements, and avoid assuming the same working-capital release repeats every year.

At exit, a buyer will test whether the improved days are operationally durable or merely the result of quarter-end collection pressure, delayed purchases, overdue suppliers, or depleted safety stock. The company should show segment-level histories, stable service and supplier metrics, documented policies, forecast accuracy, and performance through seasonal peaks. A normalized closing peg may return proceeds to the buyer if the business cannot sustain its delivered balance. The board should therefore track both cumulative cash release and structural drivers. Durable conversion supports lower net debt and a more financeable asset; cosmetic extraction invites a price true-up, QoE challenge, or credibility discount.
